In the Great Writers series, published by Mr.l Walter Scott, we have for the current month the Life of Frederick Schiller by Mr. 11, W. Nevinson. This is a volume which will tat welcome to students of German literature; for, in Widitloll to giving a readable record of the career of the great poet, it furnishco a valuable account of his imsition in relation to contemporary German writers and eon- temporary German thought. Schiller hail a lofty html. and, as he was free and fearl.s in expression, he hail an ilMtlefloe influence, especially over the youth of his time. There is a great difference in point of art between "The Robbers "unit " William ' Tell"; but they are alike in this—that they are both passionate in their love of liberty. Mr. Nevin- son has given a good account of Schiller, and pro- . ducts! an interesting book. Ursula's tact never failed her, though she was sometimes at her wits' end, elmeially when she could no longer keep the fact irons Raymond that a sentence of seven years at Toulon hail been passed on Dubois. The .worierge hall been careless enough to let out this piece of information, and if Ursula had ' been less brave, she would have I.een cowed by the menace in her brother's eyes when he dared her to say that the piece of gossip was trite. " I can only say the troth," she answered, know- ing that he must bear to hear it sooner or later ; her frank earnest eyes beneath their level brows meeting the scowl of his threatening ones. Then his fortitude altogether broke down, and till the outbreak ha.l exhausted itself her magnetic in- fluence ceased. It was as if a spell had been with. drawn. Raymond had never known that modera- lion in passion which " Hercule:, beating the air V cannot understand. Mere noise, mere deelaination, "tear a passion to tatter," And as her brother be. trwil his French upbringing, pacing the room with rapid strides,wringing his hands with frantic gestieu- latiotm, and bundlng into manineal laughter, Ursula could only wait till the fit was over.

How dear and . good you are to tne looking up with a new ex- pression in las elmaient dark-blue eyes as she stroked his hair ittol held his hands, soothing him with gentle voice mu mother might have done. Afterwards, with another sudden change that alarmed her, he askisl in a low tone, •• Do you think it possible that I shall go mad ?" . ' • • • '

moo She did not lose her presence of mind, but an- swered, smiling— " I have heard that when people ark that question they are always safe to keep their semais." Her patience was unwearied. She had heard of the gentle rubbing system u.eil by the Americans, and began strokiiig his forehead with her cool fingers, a practice which 'she sometimes kept up for the hour together—sometinies, however, holdinglois hands tight in a sudden great fear, her face pale, her lips closed firmly. His own five was so prematurely worn and lined that had it not been for his beautiful eyes it sometimes • seemed to her she would seareely have known hint • for her once singularly Ilan& cue brother. ! He Wa,l aware of the change liiinself and tohl her that lie wondered she did not shrink from his repul. sivenem.

si• "Do you think I care for babyish, unlined faces?' cried Ursula. impetuously, drawing him again tenderly to herself. It was in some such attitude that Fielding found her when lie was shown in upon her after his hurried journey from London. Ile had not counted on seeing her with her queenly head bowed, or on hearing the pathetic sound of the veiee, which was soft and tender in hlri pmdigara ears, like the cooing ai a stork dove over its young. He did not think Raymond was worth it. Yet involuntarily the words recurred to his memory—

•• She is a won :in—one in whom The mpringthue of linn eltildkh years flatl,nnr lost its (rash perfume, Thonah knowing welt that Ole hath room For many Wights and many twit," "Forgive me," he said hoarsely, "I only heard of this on Sunday afternoon." " And this in Monday—you same soon." "Von, I travelled of room all night. It wax my carelessness in not reading the papers. I was no busy in London or I ought to have heard before. I never looked at the l'aris news."
Both of them irtanee,l at haymow'. Was he annoyed at Fielding's coming. or was he in a ctate past annoyance when nothing inure could trouble him ?
—Tinhling saw in a moment that the veins of the eye- balls were injected with blood, and that the lips were blue and gniverino. "• • •
" Will 'you let Ns wreck ell the good in you, Ray t " lie said, stooping down Cl and speaking as he would to a child.

" If I had put an end to myself before it happened, it would have been better for everyone hot I've been the unluckiest of dogs," the other muttered. And then with a sudden burst of passion, " But I sill not have your pity, though you pretend to care for me. Feu have no need to preach to tee, I used to preach myself o little While ago. I know you will despise ace—you can't possibly help it. It's a part of your—way of showing your goodness." It was a little hard on Fielding, who prided him- self on never preaching to any one. But for the next few days Fielding's diplomacy failed him as Ursola's had failed before, and yet few men could have been more tilted, in the largeness tif their charity or in limitless patience, to cope with this form of despair- ing weakness. Few young men knew more, alas! about this diseases of human hearts and the intrigues of this w:cked world without being themselves drawn into the slough than Fielding did. It had saddened him, and accounted for that look of experience in his , thoughtful face which seemed to contradict its otherwise youthful appearanm. He had not yet, I reached his thirty years 1111 earth. Vol that look told I , of an insight prematurely brought to bear on this di.oriaird and criminal humanity—an insight which had taught him that lie was not impeccable himself, but that all of no had more or less been shipwrecked, or hail failed in endeavour, so that there was little opportunity left for mutual recrimination. Tile world is often ruthless 'because it is wicked ; it In hard u,pon the sinner because it sins itself. But in Fielding ease there Walt DO route left for hardness. " When a 111 all has been ollell 41 rock," he thought, looking pitifully at Raytnend, "it is as if all the devils in hell were dragging hint iloon against his better self ; it becomes another forni of physical disease, and the ellen of the struggle is greater than we can guess." To Ursula he only said— "We most get yene brother away. His nervous system is no utterly broken down that it is tselese to argue with him when he is in Ws pre:scut stete. It was AS he said. The ne.slle in the compass no longer pointed truly ; the whole mental balance had been upset in Raymond's ease. The tints had come when the everlasting combat had began to sick...the tired man, when the game did not seem worth the I candle, and when Raymond felt as if it would he better en surrender all that was at stake than to gain victory by eonstant wrestling with himself. The ten- tore of his days had lately seemed to be made up of jarring colours r the ideal musie which he had coveted Ihad rasolved itself into dissonanee. Bet though his teeth were were net on olguand Iris oars were jarred, I he seemed to have lost the taste fur the harmony he ! had once desired.

Fielding flushed. His indignation, hitherto con- trolled, got the better of him, when Ursula was mentioned in this way.

" No," he said, sternly, "it to impossible for con to digraee her. No one has really the power to dis- grace another—we are the arbiter., of nor own lives." " But people will say it—as yen well know." "Let ti say what they will. A few, at least, will keep from joining in the canine whelps which cannot hurt her." _

In ninny cases repentance has it; -shifts to ela.a: pionshment ;ii, others the stripes follow quickly on the offence, promptly and perhaps mercifully. But : sooner or Inter suffering should be over for the ; repentant. In Raymond's ease there seemed to he neither of these usual alleviations. So lung as Dubois sentence lasted,so long did lie feel no if he I were :tied by a chain to the convict and doomd e Ito stiller with hini, pang for pang. The rement- I ;ranee of Valentine Borand—deprived in her girl- hood of the enjoyments of exiidenee -seemed to snake it nectsc;ary,for him to cense to enjoy his own youth. Fielding had never cared for the poor fellow so notch as when he detected WIN in wearing a hair shirt under his other clothing..

It was useless to argue with him on the absunlity of this attempt to bury the :senses, which crop up in abnormal fornis,coming back like seven devilti,ntore powerful than before useless to assure hint that itecetieimut in its reactien incant tyranny, violence, and " felodle.se !" " You know that I "at a munlerer—that the moral : guilt is mine." "I only know that it will be another firrn of murder if your ONVII nnothoml hits to be slain," Fielding had answered, protesting against the false idea that a false opinion becomes true by continually reiteratine it. • ' ' •

'At an rate we have made much progress. Take courage at the thought that his worst enemy -T-the drink—is being kept at bay," be had said, with a cheery mile to Urania, ashe left Parisfor He did not add that when he had made the same observation to Hay the latter had answered with ,one :of those smiles which scented now to be no part of him, that treat least, would soon cease to need "relay horses for further travel." "No doubt he has had a very violent shock—a very terrible one." Fielding had admitted, " but he will brisk up and get fresh tone in the clear reviving air." Nor did he think it necessary to increase the sister's cares by repeating to her what the invalid had said to hini—t hat he felt it \VAS of no good struggling further. He had always been feeble. Had never carried lilt his resolutions. He seemed to be aware of it now, when he fancied that death WaS drawing near. He had always known what wao right, and had never been able somehow to do it. It might be better to make a fresh start in the other world—better anyway—he bad soul in a sudden fit tif confidence. Fielding had thought it better to say nothing about all this, though he saw inquiry in Ursula's face. He himself hall had something to conquer, for be had met Grandet nail good friend, and had shaken hands with bin more than onee iii UrstM's presence, even thanking the supposed sweetheart for coining. He had, perhap, wondered a little in his secret heart that the Frenchman was able to treat the matter exactly as he did, and that Grandet should care no more for the family disgrace. But it was not a time for talking of marriage, or giving in marriage —Raymond's condition brine, no Dr. Havarti 11.01 admitted, when consulted about 'it by letter, for too critical.

Fielding had, indeed, hastened away more than once when he found Ursula sitting with Louis Grandet and her brother because he would not dis. ; tar!, the sacred privacy of a family. I Every one smite of Raymond just then in a pitiful tone but with a forced cheerfulness, and the nick man knew well what they meant by their pity. He no longer talked --as lie had once talked, when connected with the Sal vationists—notchaliont religion. He hal not acted these things out in life, and he did not like to talk of them in sickness.

Once only he said to Fieldiag, " Oh, you will believe RIO now ! Dying people toll no lies—arid I never wished to hurt Valeniine Durand, though I mid I wished she were deal—dying people at least can be left with their Maker." He was brave for the first time; his manner bad gained dignity. Alla if Ursula suffered unteli slip iii net hing, to any human erratum. No one was near enough or clue enough to be trusted at this crisis.

The return fixture between the above organizations took place on Saturday, when the Warringtonisns journeyed to Wakefield. The weather was sadly against a good disphy of football, and naturally interfered with the attendance, and at the time to kick- off there would probably not to more than 200 people proont. Neutral ground was the seene of operations non after the restart, but a quick forward movement of the Tykes was more than equalized by a tall punt by Frank Turner. Booth dropped out., and neutral ground was again the scene of operations. Barnes secured Brannan before he could make headway, but a good pass to Mime almost ended in the Wakefield man scoring. Hutchinson endeavoured to get in, but without avail, and at this juncture of the game snow fell in large flakes, so that the onlookers presented a pretty sight as compared with the players, who were nosy literally covered with mud. From a pack near the Warrington line Ilutchinsio raced across the ground. and on being tackeld he judiciously 1i:tool to Falb., who grounded, the kick at goal being a failure. Warrington now put in a spirited nosh, and a kick by Frank Tamer forced another minor. The annexe,l letter is extracted from the canons of the San Francisco .Mo 11l i l eall." It will be semi that Mr. Whitham has still a warm corder in his heart for his Countrymen, and that lie is eager as ever to strike a blow against political intoler-

, , Sir.—Allow me hi mix. my hat with the utmost respect to "A French-American." I thank him tir the kindly manner in which he refers ti my nmarks, and, while I pull up stakes and coil the ropes so as to stop further ' "sparring," I also thank him fir one, tie-ins manner in which hora nie to pluck one or two feathers from the wings id spreacheagleism." I grant his argument 'with pleasure. If Igoto a •• firsts-lass house they znav sleoir me English goods, but If I want the best it Is litrrnian or French even time." We will not fallout about the quality—let it fulfil, that we love formed me thing, and that is, that the best of everything ill our drt•-goods stonw isimported. I hope.. . American fellow-citizens like the gracious condescension of my French friend ; at all events, I must re-echo his words, and say "If American manufacturers make the sainc 'ingress f,,r the next few years under protec- tion, which they have done in the past, ;here will ix.n be no occasion for any dealer hi attempt to pass off native manufactured goods fir • English you know.'" My position resins I, be pretty good, and, put in plain English, 'lran my Freneh-American friend puts it oilcans all the best goirts in our stores are imported but if American manufarturtrs will only exert themselves, this very unsatisfactory state of things may soon Ise obviated. Well, my pious wish is that tins exertion may Conllnenee at once, although I ant at a loixs to know what they have betql about SIJ long in the State of Slas,bihusetts, Whieh claims to be a second Lanca- shire. _ . .

friend is slightly wrong When he says Ainerirans go to England to speisl money. They go for another purpose, not mike so laudable, and that is to hy thsir fishes at ths feet of some pennileas pauper, such as the links of Marlboro. True it is, also, that wsalthy Americans go to spend mossy, they also go to Paris. Hams of them are to be found at the German spas, hut what of that ?

And now, Mr. Editor, allow are to state my case, and in doing to may I first say that I protest against quotations being given from English Society journals. , They do not represent the English masses. They know nothing of the intmsely strong and friendly feeling which permeates the English pimple towards their kin I beyond the sea. A strong Republican feeling is growing lup among the English working classes. They an. keenly airy, to the uselessness .4 an idle and pauperiwal aristocracy. For twenty years their eyes have con- vinced them of the fact that a gilded throne and a nwptre of geld act just as well the part of monarch as the most costly piece of humanity. It is this admira- tion for American institutions by the English working- men which masperatm those wfio toil not, neither do they spin, and which, finding its vent in the nwiety journals, gets quoted in Amerimn jourmds as the opinions of Englishmen. tam thankful to the lady "C. C." who, in the Woman's Column, disclaims any intention on the 'art cl Anwrirans to ',lsn't English- men in their adopted land. I sow.ce it is a fact that Englishmen an. self-assertive. Is it not also true that America's foremost nu-n and women, desrendanta as they are of English stock, have the name distinguishing features ? I take it that our duty in to cultivate the true cosmopolitian spirit. We, itntnigrants from all the nations of Europe, who have nought this land with an eye to the main chance," have nothing to gain by hurling abusive epithets at the various lands of our birth ; then let it drop, and let us see what steps we can take to make thin corner in. the West as golden in reality- as it is in name. Sin, this correspondence arose I have received the most abusive of tetters through the post. lam satisfied as to the nationality of the writers it is " English ye know." and tint brings me to the I question In the liberty so much boasted lof in the : Staten, a reality? I think not, or why nhould I, through fear oi " tool " he intitnidated into witholding my real signature ? There snails to he. feeling ainong a certain clam of people, something akin to that which all.wts schoolboys on being hat Out of school—a newly acquired feeling of liberty which impels them to go to the nearest toy- store and buy something, no matter what. With a man. who has not put away childish thoughts, a pistol is bought, and tragic conse- quent,. ensue. I insist that true liberty is only consistent with an eartimt wish to injure none, In the press, an able editor looks after this ; at the voting booth the policeman is called in. No true man, whatever his nationality, depends upon a shooter to give pia to his argutnent. I ant sure America has nothing to lose by Englishmen, Frenchmen, i.e Germans, on their arrival I, at once striing to get into the run of its civil and political life. The injury will conie when each nationality seeks to make America the battlo-ground for tile party strife we ought to have left behind us.

Free trad:may. or may not he good for England, but' what have I to do with that now ? My duty is to find out would it be good for the United States of America. What interests unman' is how shall we keep American politics clear of foreign influencer. Clearly no influences which the voters possess can accomplish this, On long as he remains under the influencesof a party boas. Corruption in politics has worked out the European workman's ruin. Shall it also ruin the American work- men ? Cannot an independent party he formed, and taking into its bands all municipal, or State affairs, work out its own redemption Now, tin. I hope I have made it clear to readers of "The Call" that love forms native land does not blind me to her faults, neither slav it render one incapable of doing his duty in Ids adopted home. It may loe that the !" true American" may come to see that even this favored land is not without its blemiNhes. When this in • done, cleansing what I call the Augeon stable may be , commenced. 11. Tex Government have had to cave M with regard to their treatment of Mr. W. O'BRIEN ; the storm of indignation which has burst upon their heads has been too much for thorn; and the result is that the member for Cork neither wears the felon's dress, nor is he furnished with felon's fare. Mr. single-handed, has again beaten Mr. listromi, backed though he is in , Irehiel by an army of soldiers and policemen.l The IRISH gECREIi."LI is taught that there is a power in public opinion whi,± is beyond that of batons and bayonets—that the great forces of the world are moral and not physical. The public meetings which have been held spontaneously throughout the country have everywhere been largely att.:tried : and Vim, is now as much feeling on the Balfourian an there was on the Bulgarian atrocities. Warrington contributed its share to the volume of protest at a crowded meet- ing held in Wycliffe Hall, on Wednesday night. Mr. JOHN CROWD:LI), who occupied the chair in I the absence thr, ~, gh illness of Mr. McMiNNuts, the President of the Liberal Association, struck a deep chord in the powerful protest which he made in opening the proceedings. Other speakers followed in the same strain, the meeting show- ing itself keenly responsive awl sy.npathetie. Resolutions were passed condemning the Irish Executive, and thanking the Mayor and Mayoress of Manchester for their generous treatment of Mr. YBRIEN. Unfortimately,the Mayor of Manchester is not showing himself equal to continuing in the right counie. At a meeting of the City Council, on Wednesday, he made a weak surrender of principle in order to obtain temporary peace. He commenced business by expressing his regret that his treatment of Mr. °Tants at the Town Hall did not meet with the general approval of his fellow °Rise.. This ieight mean little or it might mean much, and that it meant much was shown by the following motion being immediately moved from the Tory side of the chamber :--" 'Flint this Council accepts with pleasure the explanation of the Mayor as hi the recent entertainment of Mr. W. O'BRtax, and records its deep regret that the incident should have omurred.' The motion was seconded, put to the meeting, and adopted before the bulk of the members of the Council understood what had happened. That the Mayorshould regret that he could not please everybody is intelligible enough ; but that he should be party to express- ing regret" as to the recent entertainment of Mr. O'BRIEN" is not intelligible, except on the ground that he haa lost his head in the burly-burly of the hour. His worship doubtless thinks that what he has done makes for peace. He will find that he has cried peace when there is no peace, and that he will be despiaed rather than honoured for turn- ing his back upon his better nature. But Man- chester is right, however far the Mayor may go wrong; and the country is right. If there axinld he an election next week, there can be no ques- tion that the Government would be ignominiously hurled from power. We are glad, therefore, to non that the National Liberal Federation is moving ! in the direction of promoting petitions to the Queen for the dissolution of Parliament. The members of the Governinent will, we know, cling to offito as long as they can; they dare not faee the constituencies they have betrayed. Their doom, however, in fixed, and it is 801110 satisfaction to realise that the longer the stroke is delayed the more certain and the more severe, in the end, will be their punishment.

WE had occasion is few weeks ago, in con- sidering London sm ke in relation to London fog, to point out that the latest researches in chemistry show that the dust-mirticles in the air are found to be enormously increased in a vitiated atmos- phere as compared with as atmosphere comparatively pure. Experiments, it was pointed out, had been made to ascertain the number of organic and inorganic dust-particles in a cubic inch of air; and in view 44 the germ theory of dis- ease it is obviously of the highest importance to obtain accurate data on such matters. Paoressoa GAUTIER, teacher and lecturer on chemistry before , the Facult6 de Dttklecine of Paris, seems to have , been pushing inquiries in this direction to some purpose. He has recently published a textbook on inorganic and organic chemistry which, according to the " WJstininster Review," (which devotes an article to the work, goes far beyond English text books in " connecting the results of chemistry with !their technical and hygienic applications." Knowledge is power only when it is brought into use ;and it would seem that the knowlmlge we are , gradually acquiring of bacteria and all their ways I will, Wore many years are over, have far-reachh ig results in the prevention of disease. (granting that the genii theory is true, how startling becomes the statement that, while the air out at sea is !almost free fropi bacteria, the air of a city may be said to be alive with bacteria. Taking a cubic metro of tar as a basis of comparison—that is a cube of nearly forty inchen—Professor GAUTIER finds bacteria in the air as follows

Byron, like a true poet, presaged a truth which science explains and demonstrates when he exclaim.'
Oh, there is sweetness in the mountain air, And life that slothful ease can never share.

We have long seen the model analysing the water we drink ; and we are beginning to perceive the importance of knowing something more of the air we breathe. When the inquiry is further advanced, ! the Registrar-General will tell an not only the ! mortality of every town in the kingdom, bet side byside with this information he will give the per- centage of bacteria.

" aport to have the engineer hoist with his own petard," and it is, therefore, sport for Liberals to see how the Tories are dished in the metropolis in the election of Aldermen for the London County Council. The election took place on Tees- day, and,with the exception of Lord Meath, every- one of the mew Aldermen is a pronounced Liberal. His lordship is a reformer in social matters, and he, too, may be described as Liberal, even if he is not recognised as a member of the Liberal party. What makes the result nil the more galling to the Tories is that the Aldermen, without a single exception, have been chosen from outside the Council, no that the chance is denied them of gaining a seat here and there by concentrating their forces, as they meant to do, if gaps had been formed in the Council through selections from within. They consider that they are lmadly wied, and we cannot deny that the result is un- eatiefaetery—to the Tories. But there is a soul of good in things evil. They will, perhaps for the first time, realise that the Aldermanic prin- ciple is an unsound principle, arid ought to be swept from the political board. Liberals iii the Home of Commons strongly protested against the provision for the election of Alder- men when the Loud Government Bill was in progress. But the Tories were in a majority; they would have their own Wily; and they are deservedly punished by being beaten with their own stick. It will be something new for the Liberals to he in the ascendant in London. It is to be hoped they will work well together, and keep the hold they have obtained. It will be their 4,wn fault if they do nit maintain a majority for many years. It will make the Tories so nick of the word " alderman " that, in the end they will, be glad to assist the Liberals in striking it out of the statute book.

What is known as the Bradford tragedy has assumed allow phase; a coroner's jury has brought in a verdict of 'wilful murder" against the milk- man Barrett. It was thought that,wlien the magis- trates had disraiased the charge, there would he an end of the matter. It is the new wan.. Dyer : who has given a turn to the case. He swfmrs that he saw Barrett on the morning when the remains of the boy Gill were discovered, carrying a parcel, and spoke to him, sifter which Barrett went in the direction where the hody was nhortly afterwards found. Thin is certainly material evidence, and the ease undoubtedly requires further investigation.

THE TREATMENT OF POLITICAL
PRISONERS.

NDIGNATION MEETING AT WARRINGTON. EXTRAORDINARY PROCEEDINGS. As a protest against the treatment, by the Irish Executive of Mr. W. O'Brien, Ml', and other political prisoners, a public meeting was held on Wednesday evening, in the Wycliffe Hall, Warring- ton, at which great indignation was expressed at the recent action of the Government. The chair was taken by Alderman John Croatleld, J.P., and the large hall WON crowded. Amongst the gentlemen who accompanied Mr. Crostleld on the platform were Mr. E. J. Guest, J.P., Dr. Gomel', J.l'., Coon. 11. Roberts, and Messrs. T. Birchen, T. Morrie, John Walker, W. Roberts, F. Roberts, F. Loughlin, J. Gandy, Cornea', Pickavance, .8. Plinston, S. Kenyon, S. Jones, E. Whitehead, J. Harrison, E. Wright, J. McConville, W. Walker, IL Chambers, J. Manilla, Jordan, G. Holton], W. Stirrup, and J. Clayton, Liberal agent. Amongst those who occupied seats in the body of the ball were the Rey. Father Thompson, Alderman Holmes, Councillor Garner, and Messrs. C. J. Holmes, J. Kean, J. Haynes, M., Knowles, T. Miller, H. Eyes, H. Clayton, D. Tinnion, I'. Caldwell, S. Barlow, E. Plinston, J. Craik, O. Clay, G. Weaver, T. Eden, 3:e. The CHAIRMAN, who was received with cheers, said he was exceedingly sorry to hear that their dear friend, Mr. McMinni., was laid up at home, ill with gout, and he (the Chairman) had pursuaded him not to attempt to come out and attend that meeting. because it would really he serious, perhaps, for his health, and he knew that under those cireurnstance.s they would all of thorn excuse him. (Hear, hear.) He told Mr. McMinniuzs if he would atop at home he would willingly take his place at that meeting. (Applause.) He should call upon the Secretary to read letters of apology at the commence- ment of the meeting. Mr. CLAYTON (secretary) then read the letters. The Sent was dated " Sommer House, Warrington, Feb. Bth, 1889," and was as follows : ••My deer Mr. Croafield,--I regrot Skull am not able lota prrAelat at your meeting to-night, at I Sc, suffering trom an attack of gout. I agree entirely with the object of the meet- ing. and join readily in the cindenmation of the Government in its treatment of Mr. O'Brien and the Irish patriots. I was pleased to see that the Mayor of Manchester treated this socalled criminal with so much courtesy and hospitality. I hope that the time is not far distant when we may see Ireland treated with a policy of conciliation instead of cruelty. Hoping that you may have a successful meeting.—l am, yours faithfully, 111. McM for I rm."

Councillor F. A. Roberts, writing from Cardiff, said —"I: should have felt It a prli (lege to have added my vote in favour of the proposed resolutions. though It seems impossible to put into soffieiently expressive language the abhorrence with which every true-bearl el man moist view the treatment by Mr. Balfour and his Government of our fellow subjects In Ireland. Much as we deplore the sufferings of Mr. O'Brien, and protest against the gross indignities to which he has been subjected, may tee not hope that this inhuman treatment will to rouse the people of this country to a sense of their responsibility in allowing the continuance in office of this Coercion GoVernment. that they will &AVM an Immediate appeal to the constituencies before such conduct be repeated !or continued. I trust an. In the meantime. whilst doing cur utmost to promote this end, let us express our sympthy with nor l'sio'rh,tl=tahrermhfociepprethsosedgt; and let It he thut in future their Muse shall be our CAWe. At all events that is my determination." Writing front London, Councillor P. H. Fleming said that the Indignation that Mr. O'Brien', imprisonment had excited was already bearing goret fruit for the mune which they all had at heart. All honour to him for his determination not to submit to the brutal and retie] indignity heaped upon him by Balfour and his minions. The Mayor of Manchester deserved their warmest thanks for his humane treatment of Mr. O'Brien. Mr. Robert Garnett wrote that bethought the t rent inent of Mr. O'Brien by the Government more degrading to the Government than to the peesrrn who suffered the Infliction. He trusted that the spirit now being aroused throughout the country might lead to milder and more judicious measures. The Rev. John Yong, who was to have been one of the speakers. was unable to he present in consequence of having taken eclat!. He wrote,however. saying that he believed the whole policy of the Government to Ire as inexpedient WO un- just AR OS most recent application had been brutal and inhuman. Perhaps this latest episode In the miserable history of Injustice waild help to drive the conviction home to the electors of Great Brit: ' that this state of things most In brought ton speedy end. Mr. O'Brien was not criminal. In any true sense of the wool. He defied an unrighteous law. that had been passed by a politica inrre for a nolltical end, and in so doing brok his place among a brilliant company of men in all ages, who dared to do right. aithoUgh Unjtat law branded them as criminal for so doing. He hoped the moot, me wonlil help to spread the feeling to rap dly growing that Balfourism must come tuna end, and a policy of conciliation, justice. and brotherhood be initiated. c Our friends on the other side of the way may say we am sympathising with criminals, • wrote the Rev. W. Graham. and if resistance to wicked arid unjust laws was criminal, he added, they were in good sampany. The fley. Edward Moore, consideml the attempt to brand political opponents as felons, and to degrade them by petty insult, as eowardli-, and utterly contrary to that spirit of (air- play which Englishmen pmfessed so love. He believed that the country was getting disgusted with this specimen of o resolute government." An early dissolution of Parliament, modification of the Septennial art. and a generous measure of Hoine Rule for Ireland under the direction of Mr. Gladstone. should be the objeets of their ernest and urgent demand. Mr. RIM Armitage wrote Mining in hearty denunciation of the despicahle tyranny of the present administration. Mr. Balfour had found that he hail overpassed the limits of the nation's patience ; and recent events had greatly strengthened the muse of Home Rule. The Osamu., who wasraceived with ss)arna applause, said : I stand on this platform not only as a Liberal but on an Englishman ; I stand here 10 pmtest with all the strength that I have in me against a en.' and wicked Government. The Tory members brind William O'Brien as a law-breaker. The law that lie has broken was obtained by fraud. (Applause.) When the election of 1880 took place the Tory candidates and Liberal deserters said that they had given over with coercion and that they would not support it again. (Hear, hear.) But immediately they got in the House Of Commons, and found that they had a majority, they passed a cruel, wicked, unwarrantable, and un- justifiable bill of coercion for Ireland. (Applause.) It was a bill I would break himself. (Applause.) It was a bill that, if it were attemptGl to inflict it upon England, you Lancashire men, with me, would rise like one man against it. (Hear, hear.) I would head a riot mymlf against such a hill. (Laughter and applause.) Mn. Chamberlain, at Biriningham—(" Oh, Oh ") spoke of Balfour as a man of courage l I say that Balfour is a coward and a malignant coward. (Hear, hear.) He has got no courage in him. (Laughter and applaum.) I have lived long enough to have heard language spoken in Manchester, in 1 the Nree Trade Hall, by John Bright, as strong and I vehement against English landlords as ever William O'Brien spoke against Irish landloas, and I say this, in the face of day, that they had then as much right to take John Bright out of the Free Trade Hall and clap him in prison as they have to take William O'Brien. John Bright said in those beautiful and eloquent words of his, and I think Mr. Bright was inspired when he said them —when he plmded for " jut laws justly administered." (Applause.) Was there any justice at filitcheLstownj?

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRITAWY 9, 1889.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRITAWY 9, 1889.

(" No, no.") Was there any justice when they beAr UD William O'Brien because he condemned the landlords of Ireland for trying to squeeze Out of the poor tenants the arrears of reUt which were excessive ? The Land COM. IMS proved that the rents wereexcessive because they have reduced the rents from 25 to 50 per cent. The landlords demanded exce)sive armor: from tenants whO could not possilgy ;it was a monstrais and inigni- tons thing mei no, Englishunsl ought to rise as one man :Ind protest against it. (Applause.) It makes my Wood boil wßli indignation when I think of those things. Wm. O'Brien a law-breaker ? Why, that
~,Lil,laneet,..f,tintnlp.leii who with daintjes. bre,t it of his field withWooll

was a lea-breaker vet Ile wan also one of England's greatest heroes. The finest men we have ever had in England have been law-breakers, becant,e they have resisted inrinst laws. What is the rea.,n why we in England are peaceable ? It is because we have-justice, and justiee i, greater than law. (Bear, lunar.) Those puny mikyahle, benighted Tories—(laughter)—and laterals deserters, have forgotten that (love is such a thing as justnce. JoAnne Is higher anal loftier and nobler than any law. I thank heaven that I have got in my blood some of the old spirit of the Qualmnrs. (Applause). In days gone by there were , many of the Society of Friends who suffered in camera- , thin and punishmentand almost death before they would ober' a cruel nunl wicket and unjust law, and we that 1 live :to-day—we that have got religious and political free- -1 dont in this country, we owe it in a great measure to the exertions and the sufferingsof those noble ohm, mean- (seen of the Society of Friends. (Applause). I hope and 1 must that we, the sons of our forefathers, are not 1 going to be degenerate, hut that we will stand up and resist a cruel and wicked government like this. (Inky hear). Ireland wants conciliation not smelts ; Ireland wants the policy of our great leader William Ewart (iladstone. (Loud applause.) Ti, his everlasting honour bent recorded that that Inaris heart beats in sympathy with his fellowmen, and he doe:: no: confine it to Englishmen, but his heart goes over to Ire- landandhe says toils- Insh people," I will help you "and the Irish people believe him. (Applause.) This Balfour, this miserable lialfour—ffaughter)—boasts about thin- contentment of Ireland and the batter intssof prosperity of the country and of more money in tine nn virn„s banks. Re may stop boasting ; what peace there Is in Ireland is due to nn—the Liberal party. (Hear, hear.) It is because the Irish people,—theNationalist leaders of Ireland—know that we, the Liberal party inn England, have gotsympathy vrith them, and it is because they believe that we will do justice to them and that we will free thesn from the tyranny under which they are oppressed that snakes them a contentssltsmtge at the prisent time. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Lord Salisbury may try his resolute govern- ment for 20 years, or he may try it for 200 years, but he would never ronquer tine Irish people, and cf I was living in Ireland and an Irishman I would tell hint to kin face the same thing ; he should never conquer nne. Just to think that they have 30,000 of the military in Ireland and I don't know how many policemen, Stan expense of L 4,000,000 a year, to keep down these people, to crush them, to compel them to obey a wicked and unjust and unwarrantable law. (Shame.) Is it not enough to make an Englishman's blood boil? (" It ought to boil") I did rejoiee to see that magnifieent meeting in Man- chester, in the Free Trade Hall. It was a credit to Man- chester. It reminded me of the days of 1845 and 1848, 1 when John Bright and Richard Cobden condemned the English land lairs; and I say all honour to the Mayor of Manchester—(applause)—when he treated Win. O'Brien with courtesy and hospitality, as he was entitled to receive hint, because Wm. O'Brien was not a criminal— he WAS only a political prisoner (Rear, hear.) The " Times" newspaper—. oh, oh. )—I called the "Tisanes" newspaper last year in the Public Hall, the biggest liar in England. (Laughter and hear, hear.) I repeat it, and they may continence an action for libel against me to-stern-ow if they like. (Applause.) That papersaid Wm. O'Brien came away from Ireland as a stowaway. 1 (Laughter.) It moon lie, an insolent lie ; he came away on a vessel with most who were friendly towards him, and wino considered it to be an honour to have a man, a patriot, like William &Brien on board. (Applause.) He came fulfil an engagement in Manchester, and when he was in Man- chester made that beautiful and touching speech of his. a speech which went to the heart of every reasonable man. He said "0 have come to give myself up into the hands of the police." The "Timm" newspaper mid In tried to skulk out of the meeting. (Laugh(er.) If there is one thing to as English Men that is dearer than another, I think it is kWh,. it is horrible to me to think we are living under such a Government as this. I with to Heaven we could only have a general election next week. (Applause.) They are a stupid lot the Tories, but low astonished that they haven't more sense than to see that every act they are committing of this sort, in Ireland—of cruelty and persecution—is knocking a nail into their own coffin. This last net of cruelty to Wm. O'Brien in prison—tearing, the clothes off his hick and trying to force him to put on the dress of a criminal, and leaving him naked in his cell for 38 hours to starve nun plank lsed—is one of the most disgraceful ((sings recordril in the history of England. (Rear, hear). Balfour saysthat these things pass away. But that won't 1 pass away. (Hear, hear). lam thankful to see in to- day's paper that Mr. Balfour has thought a little better I about this and he has consented to allow Mr. O'Brien to 1 have his own clothes on, and to have decent food. lean I understand Wm. O'Brien objecting to put on the dress jof the criminal ; I would have objected had they taken me.and, as I think I haven little more physique than poor Wm. O'Brien, I would have given those four ward- anon little trouble. (Laughter and applause). A man being forced to pot on the dress of a criminal means this, that he is guilty of crime. Wm. O'Brien is not gnilty of crime. Wm. O'Brien has never sympathised with crime and has always condemned mime. Well then, you see the effect of this Balfour's miserable policy; you see they go and try to take ass prisoner Father McFadden, of Gweedore, one of the most respected priests in Ircland—(applausel—a man beioved by the people, and worthily beloved, a man whose heart—no matter what tine religion is—a man whose heart i$ full of kindness and sympathy to the people. (Hear, hear). This man, almost the idol of the Irish people in County Donegal, they positively go to the chapel with the policemen to take him a prisoner when he comes out fronn the service. Is it to be wondemd at that the congregation, that love and worship him, resisted the police? Nothing could be more unwise, nothing more injudicious, to my the least of it, than (ago to try and s take a beloved priest like that out of the very hands of I his own congregation. (Hear, hear.) The consequence is that the congregation resisted and the melancholy epti of it was that the head of the police is killed with a stone. We all lament such an event asthat—(hiar,hear) j —hut I say that bloodshed that occurs on occasions of that sort rests on the head of Mr. Balfour. (Hear, hear.) , I say, also, that the bland of the three innocent men that !were shot at Mitchelstown rests upon the head of Mr. Balfour. These men had nurture to do with that affair than any one of you in this meeting. We have the evidence of Mr. Labouchere, 51. P., and Mr. Brunner, , M.P., of what took place at Mitchelstown, and it is as ! ' plain as noonday that the police attacked a Peaceable meeting when they had no brminess ten attaek it, and yet this Balfour gets official statements I which give an entirely different opinion about the matter, and Ise soon that the official statements are 1 perfectly right. Of course Mr. Balfour says they are ! right, but we knew they are lies. The official statements I are not true. We have got the evidence of two men like I Mr. Labouchere and Mr. Brunner whose word is' undoubted anti, the facts of the case. Now, irrmpec- tive of politim —no matter whether you are I Liberal or Tory, whether you are Liberal Unionist or anything else, I say this deliberately, that this action of this Government is a disgrace to England. (Hear, hear.) And I call upon you, I call upon every Lancashire man to rise and protest against the cruel and wicked Government of Ireland by this wretched Tory Government. I think, if it were pomible, I should advise that there was a petition sent to the Queen to ask her to dismiss this Government from office. ' (Laughter and applause.) I just want to read to I you a few words I came across by accident yesterday. : They are the words of Charles James Fox, and these wore/ s were spoken in the year 1782, more than 1001 years ago. He was a wise statesman was Fox. Nobody disputed that s he was a long-headed, far-reaching man. ' He said these wonls, "Pin- his part he had rather see Ireland totally separated from the Crown of England than kept in obethence only by force." (Hear, hear.) Remember (hose words when the next election comes mound, and whoever you have to face as a candidate stick this into him. "Unwilling subjects were little better than enemies," (Hear, hear.) Why, in the words of that Irishman, that eloquent Irishman, Curran, "Tile moment that a slave sets foot upon the sacred soil of Britain his riming foil from him; he laid aside the halter and the goad, and hostood redeemed, regenerated, and disentbrallml by the irresistiblegenissa of universal eman- cipation." (Applause.) Yet William O'Brien, because be is an Irishman can be taken out of the heart of Manchester when any poor black nigger out of Africa would have been safe. (Rear, hear.) I ask myself, is it possikle that we are in this day of enlightment and Christianity we English people are fond of freedom and truth and shall we submit to such a (bingos this 7 I hope to goodness that, when the next general election comes, this Tory Government will Ibe swept away like chaff before the wind, and that we shall see our great leader, William Ewan Gladstone, --(applauser—restored tit the office of Prime Minister of England to do that which we want, which is justice to Ireland. (Lend applause.) ss _ _ _

A CAPTAIN DROWNED AT WESTON POINT.

Mr .1. E. Worsley, coroner, on Tuesday held an inquest at the Burial Hoard office on the body of William Allan, aged 38 years' captain of the schooner lietchtower, who had been missing since Monday, the 27th January. Evidence waajpven by Mr. E. Maywood, ahipbroker, to the effect that the doceasisl was at Ina office at 8 p.m. on the day in ques- tion and am+ then quite sober. Ile left in company with a number of other captains, and on Wednesday his son gave information that the deceased had not been on board since Monday. Several eaptainx volunteeredU statements that they saw the deceased on his way to his vemel at Weston Point as far as Fenton Hoek. As them were no suapiciens of foul play these captains were allowed to pmeoed to sea with their ships.—ffichard Luke, mariner of Men., Cornwall, deposed to finding the body in the canal, within a few yards of the Ketch- tower.—P.C. Hamersley said there were DO marks of violence.—A verdict of Found drowned " was returned. It was stated that the deceasaut had left a widow and four children in poor circuinstanctu anal the jurymen contributed a shilling each to the fund of their relief. The seamen in the docks have acted very generously, and upwards of £lO has been raised.

COUNTERFEIT COIN CIRLU LATE D AT RUNCORN. CHARGE AGAINST A THEATRICAL AGENT. A young man nained Thomas Dickson money taker at the Theatre Royal, was brought up at Run- corn Petty Sessions, on Monday, charged with uttering certain false and counterfeit coin resemb- ling half-a-crown knowing the same to be false:— Ur. E. Wynne Ilumphrey's defended.- -Wm. Bell, clerk in the l'ost Office said that about half past eleven on the morning on the 28th January, the prisoner came into the Post Office, and afterwards Mi. McCarraher, another clerk, came to him with a half-a-crown. Ile weighed it and found it was light. Mr. Davies, the postmaster in charge, Asked the prisoner where he got therein from, and he replied "The Theatre Royal, on Saturday night." Mr. Davies informed him that it was a bad coin and the prisoner replied "Oh dear me ; I was not aware of it." The prisoner then tendered a penny for two halfpenny stamps. Mr. Davies asked hini to go to the Police Station and kept the half- crown. By Mr. Humphreys The prisoner did not raise any objection to go to the Police Station—Miss Harriett McCarraliar gave evidence of a similar descrip- tion.—Wm. Allen, jeweller, employed by Mr. J. B. liankes. High-st., said lie had tested the half-crown pro- duced and found it WAS 9.1. short of a good one. Mr. Humphreys handed the witness a number of coin, and asked if those were msst ones, fie said he could not tell without weighing them. He should think Hwy wen, all bad. fly Superintendent Hollingworth He had not had an opportunity of testing this half-crown as he had the other one . Huinplireys He could Welt them as much As titian wits had them in his p.eket for hall.an-hour.— Mr. Jans4 Davies, main post inaster, also gave evidence. —lnspector O'Donnell deposed that the prisoner was brought to the Police Station. and said he had received the half-crown as part of his wages from Mr. Stanhope. Ile searched the prisoner and found upon him fld. in silver. two pennies, and a half-penny. He afterwards charged the prisoner with uttering the eoin knowing it to ton bail one. The prissier rifttied "No. 1 aid not know." Witness afterwards searched the prisoner's lodgings in Duke-at ,and also the boa office at the Theatre, but lie did not find any had coins.—ln examinatitn witness admitted that he made the search without a warrant, and said that he was never asked for a warrant. Mr. Douglas, who was at the Theatre, said Ito should not make the rehreh with 11h1 ronsent.—Mr, flumpliniys contendisl thAt there was no case against the prisoner, whose conduct thrisighout the affair showed that be was himself a victim. Mr. Humphreys was pmcceding to argue the case, when the Bench interrupted, and discharged the prisoner.
YARRTAGE OF MR, W._W. OOSSAGE, OF
WIDNES.

Mr. W. Winwood Gossage, eldest son of Mr. F. If. flos.sage, soap manufacturer, of Woolton and Widnes, was married on Tuesday afternoon at the Parish Church, Edgbaston, Birmingham, to Miss Lizzie Keen, second daughter of Mr. Arthur Keen, managing directors! the Patent Nut and Bolt Com- pany,Birmingham. The bridal party drove to church from the residence of the bride's father, Sandyfonl, I Augustus-road, Edgbaston, and the ceremony was performed by the vicar of Edgbaston, the Rev. Cresswell Strange, and the Rev. G. Astbury, uncle of the bride. The bride wore a dress of crepe de chine, with a court train of moire antique, trimmed with Brussels lace, and the orthodox veil and orange blos- soms. She was attended by six bridesmaids,dressed in unison, and carrying bouquets of white lilac. Their names were Miss Mary Keen, Mies Gertrude Keen, Miss Emily Keen, Miss Gossage, Wilan, and Mi. Dot Shakespeare. After the wedding the newly-married pair departed for London, on route for the South of France, where the honeymoon will be spent: and Mrs. Keen entertained a large com- pany, including the parents of the bridegroom, Sir Joseph and Lady Weston, Sze. The event was appro- priately recognised at Widnes. To have invited the GOO workmen of Mr. Gossage'e firm to partake of a dinner, would have entailed great inconveni- ence in business arrangements, and instead of thus commemorating his eon's marriage Mr. Gossage generously gave .CllOO towards the sick fund of the works. This fund is in reality a dividing club, of which the whole of the men are members, and the balance left at the end of each year is divided amongst the members. On Tuesday evening the senior clerks were entertained to n banquet at the Central Hotel. Mr. A. Parkes, the proprietor, cater- ing in first class style. After the repent, of which about 20 partook, the chair was taken by Mr. R. Cooke, and Mr. A. Thorpe occupied the vice-chair. The usual loyal and patriotic toasts having been given, there were duly proposed and honoured "The Bride and Bridegroom," "Messrs. Wm. flossage and Sons," "Mr. F. H. Gossage " and " Town and Trade of Widnes." During the evening a con- gratulatory telegram was despatched to the bride and bridegroom, and to their respective families. The proceedings were enlivened with songs, recita- tions, and instrumental music, and a most enjoy- able evening was spent. The foremen of the works, about 20 in number, sat down to a capital repast at the Mersey If otel, Mr. Merriman having made ample provision.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on Thursday. Mr. W. Fisher presided and there were present Messrs. 11. White, J. W. Light- burn, J. Pritchard, W. R. Itiass, F. Wiswall, J. Meadowcroft, P. Smith, W. Whittaker. E. Unison, W. Hankinson, H. J. (trice, J. Dobson; W. H. Linaker (law clerk), E. Marshall (secretary), Dr. McDougall (medical officer): W. Barker (surveyor).

HVALTII rav TOWN. The Medical Officer riposted that during last month the number 4d deaths amounted to 41. Of these one was An inquest ixsv, ant of the remaining 40 deaths 16 were due to bronchitis, 2 to whooping cough, 3 to congestion of the lungs, 2 to inflammation of the living membrane of the Main, 2 to cancer, 2 to heart disease, 2 toapoplexy, 2 to mesenteric disease, 2 to convulsions, and one each to disease of liver, consumption, inflammation of kidneys, inflammation of windpipe, natural decay, eczema, and one to premature birth. The 41 dot)ma showed an Average death rate for the twelve montlo of 271 of the estimated jompalatimom, and exclusive of the inquest ease of 28'12. The Medical Officer said the large death rate from bronchi! is, a disease over which no person had much control, was probably attributable to the incle- ment weather. The town was practically free from fevers of all kinds and was in a very satisfactory con dition.

The Highway f7r.Offiffiiiee--ffSc7X-Mnended tng Mr. Barker he relieved of the collection of the General Dis- trict Rate, the resolution to take effect front Lady Day next. The following plans were approved :—Mr. Richard Abel for the erection of three houses in Green- way-road at the Comer of Salisbury-et. Messrs. T. Kirkham and Co., for the erection of workshop and office at the top of Ellesinere-st. Mr. P. Speakman for the erection of a toolhouse at the Mount" Higher Run- t an.

..... The Finance Committee reported that the receipts for the past month amounted to £1368 160. 10d. and accounts amounting to £928 Or, 11d. were pawed for payment. The monthly statement of the General District Rate showed balance from last month £1,844 10s. 9d. amount collected in January £BOB 10s. Ekl., leaving £1,038 Reid. From thin amount was to be deducted the sum of £644 11a, a reduction on appeal, leaving the amount to be collected £393 9s. 1.1. Recommended that the General District Rate he amended by reducing the sum at which the Manchester Ship Canal -Company has been annesswl, front £10.851 to £4,405 10s. Recommended that the assinisment of Mr. T. Harrison for land at Higher Run- corn be reduced from £35 to £26 54. and that the assessment of Mr. It. Moore, Hope Hall, be struck oat of the ratehook (place of worship) Mr. Imison moved the adoption of the minutes, and referring to the reduction of the Ship Canal awessment Ire said £10,851 did not represent the figure upon which the Ihstrd had ever received any income ; it was merely! theamount to which the aaneasinent was raised. The, original amount upon which the Board received revenue I wan £5.392 12n. 64. 80 that the reduction was from I that amount to £4,405 10s. Thin wan an annual lons to I the ratepayers of £9B 14n. 3.1. The Corninittee had gone carefully into all the evidence brought before them, and they saw no other course open to them. div.head: CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL
div.p: CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL
ELECTION OF ALDERMEN.

The first provisional meeting of the Cheshire County Council was held on Thursday, at noon, in the Grand Jury-room, Chester Castle, when there was a full atten- dance of the elected councillnes--fifty-seven in all. There was also a number of persons from the city and county present, and considerable interest was manifested in the entire proceedinp. Mr. Thomas Roberts (deputy clerk of the peace for Cheshire.) opened the proceedings by announcing that the first buniues. would be theelection of n'ehairmanforthefirst andsecondmeotings of the Council. Lord F.gerten was proposed no provisional chairman by Major Antrobos and seconded by Mr. Duncan Graham, J.P. The Liberals then proposed and seconded Mr. , Duncan Graham (C), as provisional chairman on the ground that Lord Egerton, being chairman of the Court of Quarter Sessions, and also chairman of the Manchester Ship Canal, nught not to act in a dual position. Mr. Duncan Grahanisnomination received 24 supporters, while Lord Egerton, receiving 28, was declared elected. Lord Egerton returned thanks for the hmeur. A somewhat healed discussion then ensued as to the procedure over the election of aldermen. Mr. Slater Lewis (L) asked the chairman to read the list of 23 aldermen proposed to be elected ef whom 22 were E°"o'f'yofivot. Lord Egerton said if the Liberals would read their circular, signed Joseph Beckett, then he would give the list. Dr. Hodgson (L) Crewe, said that they had no objection to read the circular convening meet- ings of Liberals to discuss the appointment of aldernien. The chairman mid the first letter he sent out was private, but the second was not private. (Voice. : " Read, read.") Mr. Slater Lewis : That's your impartiality.—A Councillor, "Impertinent. impertin- ent."—The Chairman's suggestion to adjourn was then i carried.
The councillors then adjourned, and after an abmnce of three houm returned. The Chairman then announced I that they would proceed with the election of the alder- mf".

...Mr. Duncan Graham said that during the throe hours they had had repeated conferences, with Ow result that they had agreed upon a certain list of nineteen names. After other remarks the election IV TA proceeded with and announced as follows i—The Duke of Westminster, ; the Hon. W F. Tollentacho,Tarporley (C.) Mr. Christopher Kay. Davenham (C.); Mr. Edward (treenail, Grappenhall (C.) ; Mr. R. 0. Orton, Tattenhall (C.) : Me. James Tomkinson, Willingtnn Hall )L.); Mr. Francis Williams Webb, Crewe (C.) ; Mr. Thomas Hard- castle Sykes. Cheadle (C.) ; Mr. Joseph Verdin, North- wich (C.) ; Mr. Thomas Collier, Alderley Edge (L.U.) : Mr. Thomas Rigby, Sutton Weaver !L.) Mr. Alexander Bedell, Wiltuslow (L.U.) ; Mr. James Smith. New Brighton (L.) ; Mr. Ralph Bates, Stalybridge (C.); Mr. William Artnitakre, Altrincham (L.) Mr. D. Masa Hewitt, ; Nortlovich (L) Mr. Thoma.s Reeley. Dukinfield ; Mr. Samuel Hodgkinson, Marple (L.) ; and Mr. Henry , Neild, Whitley, Northwich (LIT.) ' Messrs. Bogey, Annita,ve, Collier. and Bates having been elected frorn the Council, fresh elections are necessi- tated in their respective divisions t—sin., Duckinfield (West). Altrincham. Macchisfield (borough), and (Italy. bridge (borongh second).

The council then proceeded to decide by ballot which of the aldermen, to the number of ten, should retire on the ordinary day of the election in the third year next after the passing of the Local Government Act—i.e., 7th. November, 1891. The following gentlemen were voted upon to retire :—Mr.J. Tomkinson, 30 ; Mr. F. W. Webb, 29; Mr. T. Collier, 29 ; Mr. T. Rigby, 53 ; Mr. A. Bedell, 29 ; Mr. J. Smith, 31 ; Mr. D. B. Hewitt, 29 ; Mr. T. Beeler' 29; Mr. S. Ilodgkinson, 30 ; and Mr. N.M., 30. It was decided that the neat meeting of the Council should be held at Knutsford on the 21st inst., providing the elections in the divisions were completed. A vote of thanks to the chairman roncluded the pm- ceetlings at six o'clock in the evening. It will be seen by the above report that of the alder- men eight are Conservatives seven Liberals, and four Unionists. The High Sheriff (Baron Von Schroeder) will be communicated with as MOM as possible respecting , the vacancieu in the four divisions ; and the elections will take place in the course of the next three weeks.

div.head: MR. BRUNNER ON TORY POLICY AND THE IRISH QUESTION.
div.p: MR. BRUNNER ON TORY POLICY AND THE IRISH QUESTION.

The members of the Gladstone Liberal Club and their friends had their annual soiree on Saturday night, in the Central Hall, at Northwieh. Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., presided over the gathering, and Mr. T. FL Ellis, M.P., was also present. Mr. Brunner, in a short address, congratulated these present, and the Liberals of Cheshire generally, on the good work they hail done in connection with the County Council elections, Ile regarded the results as eminently satisfactoy. In the whole county there had been elected no many pronounced Liberals as pronounced Conservatives, and when it was remembenal that in Parliament the county, including the bonsughs in it, was represented by two Liberals as against eleven Con- servatives. they would are what a change hadcome over the face of the 0000ty.—(1Iear, hear.) The Liberals of the Northwich division were busy at present electing delegates to their popidarly constituted Liberal Associa- tion. In what they did they were always open and above board What were their friends the enemy about? They did not hear snitch of the Tory democrat in that nridhtoourh,,al They did not hear much of the doings of tlio Conservative Association. It wan rather a dead- alive sort of institution. But they might depend upon it the Tories were at work, although they did not show their heads above ground. The Tories were very much like chameleons. They took a different colour at differ. ent Dines. Four rears ago they appeared to be ardent Homo Rulers, anti they continued so until they were defeated in November and December, 1885. What were they now? lie was blessed if they had not all turned Socialists. (Laughter and applause.) This scented the the inference to be drawn from the consuls proceedings of the Socialists on the one hand,and certain members of the Conservative litany on the other, in connection with Mr. Broadhurst's visit to Winsford in October last. Pro- ceeding to speak of the political situation generally, the hon, member and a good deal had been heard lately of Mr. William (I'Brien. —iCheers.) As in the Northwich division no in the Cabinet, it appeared to him that the Tories were getting ilthperate. Their desperation in this part (.f tb. cninitry took what appeared to him to be rather a comical aspect, hut in the councils of Iler Majesty's Government it was very much more of a tra- gmly than sits comedy. We had Mr. O'Brien sentenced in his absence only a few (lays ago to four months' . imprisonment, and there was the addendum, which appeared to many minds to he, merciful one, "without hard labour.' Did they know the difference between hard labour and 11,1 hard labour ? VVhy,it was merely this, that the man was put to light !ahem; but it meant this further—it meant starvation diet. And what was the offence for which Mr. O'Brien had been so sentenced ? His offence was the deliveriny eta speech of WWI the following won the passage rthelly sired against him in the infamous court in whirls he was tried If rots want a I lemon how to 114.1 with land-grabbers, ask the Primrose dames ; ask them how they deal with the Radical Rhop- . keepers mite are goilty of a tenderness for Mr. Gladstone. The Primrose dames do not go round shooting 'Boycott thern Pint heheariognf thepolice,bntthey do it athousand times more effectis,ly. When they meet them in the street they give tlism the cut direct, they leave them severely alone. Well, I suppose we also can tread the

div.head: TTIE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 9, 1889.
div.p: TTIE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 9, 1889.

Primrose path of boycotting:* Were they going to I support, or did they wish hint to support, the 'eV, which condemned a man to four months imprisonment, either : with or without hard labour, for uttering words like these ?—(Cries et "No.") Well, Mr. O'Brien, as they knew, came acmes to England. The "Times" said he came AB a stowaway. A stowaway was one who came OR board a ship without the knowledge of the captain Of the crow. Mr. O'Brien came across not as that,but as the most honoured passenger those men ever had on Math the vessel. (Cheers.) He came to Manchester last Tues- day night, and there he had a reception at the hands of the men of Mancheoter such as no Royal Prince ever received.—(Hear, lime) Ile delivered a speech which any man in this world might be proud to have uttered. He left the meeting surrounded by 200 policemen, and was marched to the Town Hall surrounded by an enormous crowd, who cheered him at every step. Ile was taken to the Town Hall in Man. cheater and there lodged in the rooms occupied not very long ago be Prince Albert Victor, the eldrat son of the Prince of Wales, and not very long agooccupied by Mr. Arthur Balfour, his opponent.—(Gruans4 Well, all honour to Manchester and all honour to its chief magis- trate. Ile wished to ask them if they would authorise him to write to the Mayor of Manchester, Mr. Alderman Batty—a name which he trusted would be honoured Mr many and many a day—thanking him for his generous hehaviour.—(Cheers.) As to the coining session of Par- liament, to, wantesl to go there authorised by them to take every legitimate and constitutional opportunity to oppose the Government at every step. This Government was the meanest, the most cowardly, the most infamous Government of modern times. What was Mr. O'Brien ? Mr. O'Brien was a man who had never spent £lOO a year upon himself; he was a man of very high culture, Oman of absolute purity of conduct, a man whose patriotism was held in honour by nine-tenths of the people who knew him. But in Ireland Mr. O'Brien was regarded as • criminal, and for what ? Because he had advised his countrymen to imitate the Primrose League. Mr. O'Brien was a criminal for saying words which he (Mr. Brunner) was free to say either in public or private. He asked them to support him in every legal andconstitutimal step he might take against the treatment of Irishmen Ma way we would never allow Englishmen to be treated. (Hear, hear.) He asked them to pass a resolution authorising him to write to the Mayor of Manchester in their name thanking him for what he did last Tuesday night.— (Cheers.) On a show of hands being taken, it was found that the meeting was unandously in favour of the resolution. An interesting programme of vocal and instrumental rausic was afterwards entered upon.

HOSPITAL AND DISPENSAItY MANAGE- MENT. (From "The British Medical Journal.") Mr. ileorge Woods (Secretary to the Longford Wire Company, Limited, Warrington., writes I read in the "Journal" of December 22nd, 1888, the paragraph headed " Hispital and Dispensary- Management. The remarks had reference to London in particular. The suggestion of Mr. Men. Coote, Secretary of the Lock Hospital and Asylum, London, could be carritel out sacs cessfully, I think, providing the proper means are employ-est. In a large number of works in England as well as in Scotland weekly contributions of a halfpenny or A penny are made, which amounts are "stopped' every pay day in the officui of the works, and the total sum is paid to two men appointed by the employer, who givm receipts for the amounts, which they personally disposit into the hospital box, which box is always kept in the office, and called for twice a year by the hospital authorities. The amounts collected by various works are published in the local papers. In some imstances the contributions are collected in this way Every Saturday the hospital box is placed at the entrance of the works, and the men as they pass out : drop into the box what they are disposed to give. Under such conditions the sum totals do not amount to much. A few years ago the published amounts given by our workmen averaged about 3s. I was ashamed of their publicity, when I knew that some improvident men were regularly seeking the aid of the hospital and dispensary, from accidents or oiherwise.

An opportunity occurred—for I knew one would, sooner or later—when I was able to tell the workmen what I thought of their voluntary contributions to the local hospital in return for the valuable aid rendered to , many of them from time to time. In one week two men were injured; one lost a finger at his droning block, and the head of another was injured by a crane handle —both accidents the result of carelessness. Neither was in any benefit society, and the hospital was their only resource. Both men were in regular employment. I called all the workmen together one dinner-hour. I placed these facts before them, and did not forget to mention their paltry contributions. I said that "if ever two men were paupers in the proper sense of the terrn, these were." I advised what I thought they ought to do. The consequence was that, at the same meeting—after I left them—they unanimously agreed that one halfpenny per week should be deducted front their wages every pay-day. The annual contribution now is not far short of £l6. Whenever an accideir occurs, however alight, the assistance of the hospital is freely given and without question. Under these conditions a workman feels that he has a moral claim upon the institutiom More provi- dent workmen, though subseribers to the hospital and dispensary, never make claim upon either, except in cases of eerious frarture.

_ . .... All tne'men apwinted by the employes of the various works to eollect these weekly sums form a hospital com- mittee. which committee delegates two members to reprosent it on the baud of management of the hospital. Every year there is a hospital concert given by the work- ing men. They have entire control of the same. It has been!mo an institution in the town. The nett proceeds of this annual concert are never less than £35. This year

The suggestion of Mr. Conte ion practical one: but it can only be carried out by the working men. They must be made personally interested. Get hold of two or three of the "leading spirits" at all the chief manufactories in London. Encourage these men in the good work : the smaller factories will soon emulate the larger one, and the final result will hen surprise. If I may judge of id the principaLs of London linos by those in the pro- vinces, I am confident that they will give the hospital authorities all the assistance poisible, for they, non rule, arm always glad to encourage amongst their workmen the principle of self-help.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL
div.p: THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL
ELLERMF,RE PORT AND INCE.

The sectiWte"naini. from Ellesmere Port to lace is just four miles in length. There are no locks, docks, or railway deviations on this section, but some difficulty is experienred in dealing with the soft, boggy soil, and with the accumulation of sludge. A great quantity of peat has been met with on this section. At Ince Bay, about the middle of the section, the building of a large sea wall has been commenced. The total amount exca- vated on this section to the end of December was, in round numbers, 1,000,000 cubic yards, of which 30,000 was Dick. This rock is dressed and stacked in the yard ready for use when necessary. There are at present employed on this section 950 men, 14 locomotives, 9 steam navvies, 2 grabs, and 4 steam cranes. STANLOW POINT MISSION. The Sunday School connected with this Mission, over ' which Mr. Cleverly presides, is well attended. 'rho whole of the temporary village consists of only thirty families, in some of which there are no school jhildren, yet the number on the Sunday school register is sixty wholers and eight teachers. The school is held twice on Sunday, and there nine two serthces in the Mission Hall, in addition to Bible classes, prayer meetings, and a night school, where the three its are taught, during the week.

div.head: ALTERATIONS AT RUNCORN.
div.p: ALTERATIONS AT RUNCORN.

At a meeting of the Runcorn Improvement Commis- sioners, on Wednesday, the Law Clerk, in reply to Mr. Meadoweroft, said he had not received any idarmation from the Acting Conservator of the klersey in regard to this matter.—At the last meeting it was stated that the Ship Canal Contractor intended to interfere with the Canal wall, and that the alteration would be prejudicial to the whole of the upper estuary. In imnsermenre he watt instructed to write. It was at first startsl that they were going to interfere with the inlets and outlets at Malcom through the Canal wall, hot when he RIM the plans at Liverpool, he learned tha• thin wt entirely wrong.—Mr. Meadowcroft That the Board had teen Linaker Quite so. The proposal was to reduce the number of" port holes theingh which the tidal water would flow into the canal, and it.iw out again no as to scour the river. Instead of three of 300 feet, they proposed to make one of 900 fort. Mr. Lightburn said it was also proposed to raise the bed of the canal 1 foot 10 inches. This had been an advantage SO far as the dock was con- cerned. but would be a great disadvantage V.O far its communication between the river and the canal was I erincernect—The Chairman doubted whether the effect would he as stated and added that he had heard Admiral Richards would not samition the alterations. Had Mr. Meadowcrrift heard anything of it.—Mr. Meadowcroft said he had heard nothing whatever. His •pinion was strtingly in favour of the alterations and it had oceurred Ito him 'that if the Commissioners were of opinion that I they would materially benefit Runcorn, that they shoitld I supDort and uphold the changes.—The Chairman mid the Board was rather nii,lol in the first instant.. ; they understand that the entrance of VP.PI3 would be efts,- : ted.—Mr. Wiswall • That is a misapprehension. It is a question which affects the tidal flow, and it is for the Conservators to decide. Nothing in the alteration would be detrimental to the interests of Ituncorn.—m• Chair- man sugeestisl that the Law Clerk should obtain all information necessary and the discussion ceased. 81-METALLISM AND TM: WORKING CLASSES.- Sir,—ln a leader last week you allude to the fact that Mr. Chaplin has given up his old hobby of Fair Trade And taken up with a new one of Dionetallism. Mr. Chaplin is a" clam" politician, and I venture to say that he is having as little regard for the interests of the masses—the wage-earning masses—in his propaganda as a bionetallist eyes he had As a Fair-Trader. Core sides tons moment what it is the bi-metallists are seek- ing to bring about. They say that gold has appreciated something like 30 pre cent, within the last 16 or 17 years—in other words that a gold sovereign will now purchase about 30 per cent, more of other commodities— including bread, clothing, be—than it did 17 years ago. This appreciation of gold they my is sos mil—especia fly to manufacturers, farmers, and landlords such as Mr. Chaplin—and they want by means of this scheme of bionetallisin to bring down the purchasing value of the sovereign to something like its old rate of 17 years ago. Now what does this Innen to a working-man who lives upon wages. Simply that his wage will, to all intents and purposm, be at once reduced hy thirty per cent. If beget 30s. a week he will, it is true, still continue to get his 30s , but the value of the money, in comparison with the things he has to live upon and which he has to purchase with his wage, will be lessened by thirty per cent. That is to may, his 30s. will go little further than 20s. went beton,. This is haw hi- metallions witi affect a wage-earner. . . . .

On the other hand, let no see how beautif tiny it will work for the wealthy manufacturer, the comparatively well-to-do farmer, and the monopolist landlord. There will hen sudden rise of probably between twenty and thirty per cent, in the price of manufactured rxiturnodi- ties and of agricultural produce, and all this enhanced price will go into the pockets of the manufacturers and farmers, while they will go on paying their workmen and labourers nominally the same, but, as far as pur- chasing power is concernial, and this is the main thing, grmtly reduced wages. It is, however, not difficult to foresee that in the end the farmer will not very greatly benefit, although it is to his selfishness and cupidity that men like Mr. Chaplin are very largely appealing. The advantages of that excellent landlonl device known us" abatement of rent" will soon manb feat themselves. As we know, a landlord now-a-days when he finds al that his tenant cannot pay the rent that has been fixed does not at once reduce the cent; he simply makes an " abatoment " office, ten, or twenty per rent. as the case may require. If, however, bn meoallism were once fairly adopted, and the farmer ban to get big prices for his produce, what would become of the" abatements ?" It needs no prophet to tell that the " abatements " will disappear, and with them most of the extra profit of the farmer. It is mid that the old Kings of France used to claim as a prerogative, the right to depreciate the coin when debts or taxes had to be paid to them, and to raise its value when they had to discharge their debts and obligati°nt to others. In other words, eupposing our present coin to have been in vogue then, they might, when they had a debt to pay, have declared a sovereign to be worth 305., and when some one else had a debt to pay to them they might have valued the sovereign at only 10s. ; so that they might discharge a debt with a sovereign which a subject could only discharge with three nivereigns. It seems to me that the bbmetallists are seeking to apply a similiar principle under the plea of a "reform" of the currency. By a sudden raising of prices, they will be able to get more for the commodities they have to sell and to pay less for tho labour they have to buy.—Yours truly, Warrington, Feb. Bth, 1889.

A person who had consec- rated was bound as in a vire ; he had no longer any con- trol over his property or his actions. THE PARNMLL CONNISSION.—At the Special Commis- sion on Friday morning, the cross-examination of Major le Carol was resumed by Sir Charles Russell. Witness said he offered his evidence last August becaum he thought the prosecution was being lamely presented. Witness spent ten days with Mr. Houston in selecting the documents produced. Witness communicated to the Home Office the appointment of Galla,qher and Lomasney for the dynamite plots. Sir Charles Russell ! asked the witness who were the four leading men in the organisation between August, 1881, and the end of 1882, and the witness gave the names of Sullivan, Hynes, Boland, and Devoy.! Sir Charles Ruesell asked about a number of the other ' persons lie had ineutioned, and the witness said that ' they were persons who were respected in America. in, 1884, the understanding between the secret and open! organimtions was very good, and there was harmonious action. The witness was next asked about the ereden- Oafs to the conventions, and said that all persons ! attending the open conventions had to have some osten- sible connection with the Land League, but he knew of bogus sets of credentials having been made out in order that members of the C.O. might be prment at the Land League Convention. Sir Charles asked for another covering letter, and the witness, after some limitation, turned to Sir eharl. Russell and asked, " Do you wish to risk the lives of men " Don't ask me any goes- tions" quickly retorted Sir Charles Russell, and on tlw witness being assured that the President would see the covering letter before it was handed to Sir Charter he undertook to produce it.

Captain Smith, of the Ca.r.g.o. Bay, has made a state- meat in which he save i—We were bound out, and were running down the Channel with the wind north-east. while the unknown strainer was sailing up the Channel. ft was not a stormy or snowy nightas has been reported. I It had been snowing early in the day, but it was entirely clear when the collision occurred. The steamer's lights were seen be the man at the lookout same ten minutes before the ciillision occurred. We had no idea that she was going to run into us. We watched her, and thought she was ,going entirely clear of on, when she suddenly altered her course and bore down open us self to cross our bow Site came on with full speed, and in spite of all we could do to save ourselves she struck at nearly right angles from starboard to port, knocking off about eight feet of our bow. The shock was so great that the iron fore mast snapped short off like a pipe stem and went overboard, carrying away portions of the rigging. Everybody thought the ship would go to the bottom in a few moments, and they took to the boats . We were about two or three hundred yards away when the big four-masted steamer threw her stern high into the air and went down nose first. without making a rign of distress or doing anything to show that a living soul was on board, and both myself and mate were surprised that tat one could be seen on the big steamer. It did look very strange. Had she been an abandoned ship she could not have been more denoted. We remained away from our barque an hour, expecting her to sink every moment. last, after the steamer went down, we went on board!, tried the pumps, and found she would float.
